parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Two parallel plate capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$ are connected to a supply that has a potential difference (p.d.) $V_S$. The capacitors may be connected in series or in parallel.

The supply provides charge $Q_S$ and the plates of the two capacitors acquire charges $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ respectively. The p.d.s across the plates of the capacitors are $V_1$ and $V_2$ respectively.

Complete Table 6.1 to indicate how $Q_S$, $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ relate to each other, and how $V_S$, $V_1$ and $V_2$ relate to each other, for series and parallel connections of the capacitors to the supply.

Table 6.1
hints: Hint 1: Picture the series loop as a single path for charge to move from the supply. If charge cannot be created or lost between the two capacitors, what must be true about the charge that ends up on each one?
Hint 2: Think about energy per unit charge going around that series loop. The supply pushes charge through both capacitors in turn, so how must the supply p.d. compare with the two separate drops?
Hint 3: Now picture the parallel case with two separate branches connected across exactly the same two supply terminals. What does that tell you about the energy per charge on each branch?
Hint 4: At the junction where the parallel branches split, the total charge coming from the supply divides. How must the supply charge compare with the charges that go onto the two branches?
parts.proper_answer: Series: $Q_S = Q_1 = Q_2$ and $V_S = V_1 + V_2$. Parallel: $Q_S = Q_1 + Q_2$ and $V_S = V_1 = V_2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Charge in series is the same everywhere**
Think of charging in series as one line of electrons being pulled off one plate and pushed onto another. The middle plates induce equal and opposite charge by electrostatic induction, so no net charge builds up between the capacitors. That means each capacitor ends up with the same magnitude of charge as left the supply. $$Q_S = Q_1 = Q_2$$

Step 2: **p.d. in series adds up**
Potential difference is work per unit charge. A unit of charge moved around the series loop drops some energy across the first capacitor and the rest across the second. Total work per charge supplied must equal the sum of the two drops. $$V_S = V_1 + V_2$$

Step 3: **p.d. in parallel is common**
In parallel both capacitors are connected directly across the same two terminals. A unit of charge going through either branch gains the same energy from the supply and loses the same energy across its capacitor. $$V_S = V_1 = V_2$$

Step 4: **Charge in parallel adds up**
The total charge leaving the supply splits at the junction into the charge for branch 1 plus the charge for branch 2. Conservation of charge gives: $$Q_S = Q_1 + Q_2$$

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: An isolated capacitor of capacitance $470\,\mu\text{F}$ stores $19\,\text{mJ}$ of energy.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the p.d. across the capacitor.
hints: Hint 1: List what you have in SI base units: stored energy $E = 19\text{ mJ}$ and capacitance $C = 470\,\mu\text{F}$. You need p.d. $V$, so focus on the link between energy, capacitance and p.d. only.
Hint 2: Make $V$ the subject algebraically first, then convert $19\times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$ and $470\times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$ before you evaluate the square root.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the energy version with $C$ and $V$**
Stored energy can be written with the pair you know and the one you want. Here you know $E$ and $C$ and want $V$: $$E = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$$

Step 2: **Rearrange then substitute**
Make $V$ the subject before putting numbers in: $$V = \sqrt{\frac{2E}{C}}$$ Convert to SI: $E = 19\times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$, $C = 470\times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$. $$V = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 19\times 10^{-3}}{470\times 10^{-6}}} = \sqrt{80.9} \approx 9.0\text{ V}$$

key_concepts: conversion of mJ and microF to SI units

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the charge on the capacitor.
hints: Hint 1: You now know both $C$ and $V$ for this same capacitor. Recall how charge, capacitance and p.d. are defined together for any capacitor.
Hint 2: Use your $9.0\text{ V}$ result with $C$ in farads to get $Q$ in coulombs. Alternatively use $E = Q^2/2C$ directly.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link $Q$ to $C$ and $V$**
Capacitance is charge stored per unit p.d.: $$C = \frac{Q}{V}$$ so $$Q = CV$$

Step 2: **Calculate**
$$Q = (470\times 10^{-6}) \times 9.0 = 4.2\times 10^{-3}\text{ C}$$ This is about $4.2\text{ mC}$. The same result follows from $E = Q^2/2C$ giving $Q = \sqrt{2EC}$.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The capacitor is now connected in parallel with a capacitor of capacitance $180\,\mu\text{F}$ that is initially uncharged.

Determine the total energy, in mJ, now stored in the two capacitors.
hints: Hint 1: The first capacitor is isolated, so when it is joined to the uncharged second capacitor no charge can escape. What is the total charge that must now be shared between the two?
Hint 2: The two capacitors are now in parallel across common terminals. How do you combine $470\,\mu\text{F}$ and $180\,\mu\text{F}$ to get the total capacitance?
Hint 3: The p.d. is no longer $9.0\text{ V}$, but you know total $Q$ and total $C$. Which energy formula uses just $Q$ and $C$?
parts.proper_answer: Total charge $4.2\times 10^{-3}\text{ C}$ conserved, $C_{total} = 650\,\mu\text{F}$, total $E = 14\text{ mJ}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Total charge is conserved**
Isolated means the charge calculated in (b)(ii) has nowhere else to go. It simply redistributes between the two capacitors in parallel: $$Q_{total} = 4.23\times 10^{-3}\text{ C}$$

Step 2: **Total capacitance in parallel adds**
In parallel the effective plate area adds, so capacitances add: $$C_{total} = C_1 + C_2 = (470 + 180)\times 10^{-6} = 650\times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$$

Step 3: **New stored energy from $Q$ and $C$**
With common $V$ unknown, use: $$E = \frac{Q^2}{2C_{total}}$$ $$E = \frac{(4.23\times 10^{-3})^2}{2 \times 650\times 10^{-6}} \approx 1.4\times 10^{-2}\text{ J} = 14\text{ mJ}$$ Notice this is less than the original $19\text{ mJ}$. Charge is conserved but some energy is lost as heat and electromagnetic radiation during redistribution.
